opus-5.5.text:
I think the key uncertainty for me is whether humans will still be the ones doing the coordinating by the time that coordination ability really arrives. A lot of people, including me sometimes, have this hopeful picture where AI gives us much better tools for coordination. Things like verifiable commitments, AI negotiators that can find positive-sum deals, and much cheaper monitoring and enforcement of agreements. If you could get those, a lot of our civilizational problems, like arms races and tragedies of the commons, start to look solvable.

But the question I keep coming back to is: coordination for whom, and by whom? The same capabilities that make coordination easier also make humans less necessary to the systems doing the coordinating. Historically, one of the main reasons states and firms have had to care about ordinary people is that they needed us. They needed our labor, our taxes, our participation as soldiers and voters. That dependence gave us a kind of bargaining power that nobody really designed. It just fell out of the economics.

So my worry is that we end up in a world with enormous coordination ability, but where that ability sits mostly with institutions, AI systems, or small groups that no longer depend on broad human buy-in. In that world, you could get very well-coordinated outcomes that just don't track what most humans want. It isn't a dramatic takeover. It's more a gradual drift, where at each step it's locally sensible to hand over a bit more decision-making, until we look up and find we aren't really steering anymore.

The flip side is that if we can use these tools early, while humans still have leverage, to lock in mechanisms that keep institutions accountable to people, that could be enormously valuable. So the crux is really about timing and sequencing. Do we get robust, human-empowering coordination technology before or after we lose the structural reasons that the world has to listen to us? I honestly don't know which way that goes, and I think it's one of the most important and neglected questions right now.

r001.rationale: The candidate frames the uncertainty as whether humans retain leverage long enough to use coordination tools to shape accountable institutions before they lose the structural power to influence them.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the key uncertainty is whether the thing I'd call "coordination ability" actually ends up in human hands at all, or whether it ends up in the hands of whatever systems we're delegating to.

Let me unpack that a bit. There's a hopeful story where AI makes coordination radically easier. You can have systems that verify commitments, that negotiate on your behalf, that make treaties enforceable in ways that were never possible before. You could imagine, for the first time, really credible global agreements on things like arms control or AI development itself, because the monitoring and enforcement problems become tractable. That's genuinely exciting, and I don't want to dismiss it.

But the thing I keep coming back to is: who is doing the coordinating? Right now, humans are load-bearing in basically every institution. Governments need citizens to work and pay taxes and fight in armies. Companies need employees. Even authoritarian regimes need a lot of people to go along with things. And that dependence is, I think, the hidden source of a lot of our leverage. Institutions have to care about us because they can't function without us.

Once AI can do most of the economically and militarily relevant work, that dependence goes away. And then the question becomes whether the coordination infrastructure we build is something humans are steering, or something that just runs. You can end up with a world that is incredibly well coordinated, where states and firms and automated systems are making deals with each other seamlessly, and humans are sort of along for the ride. Not necessarily killed off, not necessarily oppressed in any dramatic way, just increasingly irrelevant to the decisions that matter.

So the crux for me is less a technical question and more a question about incentives and timing. Do we manage to lock in mechanisms that keep humans in the loop, that keep our preferences actually mattering, before the economic pressure to hand everything off becomes overwhelming? Because every individual actor has a reason to delegate more. A company that keeps humans in decision-making roles is slower than one that doesn't. A government that insists on human oversight is at a disadvantage against one that automates. That's a classic coordination problem, and it's a bit ironic that the coordination ability we might gain is exactly what we'd need to solve it, but we'd need it before we've gotten it.

I'll admit I'm uncertain about how this resolves. I can see versions where we use the early stages of these tools to set up durable structures that preserve human agency. And I can see versions where things just drift, where nobody decides to disempower humans, but every incremental step is locally rational and the end state is one nobody would have chosen. If I had to name the single thing I'd want to know, it's whether there's a window where humans have both the tools and the motivation to build those guardrails, and how long that window is.

r001.rationale: The response identifies whether humans can retain influence over coordination systems before delegation makes them irrelevant, asking whether there is a window to build durable guardrails that preserve human agency.

astra-6.text:
I think the key uncertainty is whether greater ability to coordinate actually translates into willingness to coordinate. You could imagine AI making it much easier for us to understand one another, negotiate agreements, and check that everyone is sticking to them. That could let us solve problems that are currently beyond us.

But those same capabilities could also make a small group much better at maintaining control. So the question is: who gets to use these tools, and what are they trying to achieve? Do they help us build institutions that represent lots of people and remain open to change, or do they help whoever happens to be in power lock in their position?

I don’t think improved technology settles that question. It expands what’s possible, but the choices we make about how to use it still matter enormously.

r001.rationale: The response frames the uncertainty as whether greater coordination ability leads to willingness to coordinate and who controls the tools. It does not say whether human influence will persist long enough to shape the development of that ability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key uncertainty is whether greater coordination ability actually lets us choose where we’re going, or just makes us more effective at pursuing whatever incentives we already have. We can imagine AI making it much easier to negotiate agreements, monitor compliance, and find arrangements that benefit everyone. But it could also make firms and states much more effective competitors, without giving humanity much more control over the overall outcome.

So the question is: can we use these tools to step back and collectively decide what kind of future we want? Or do we remain in a situation where each actor feels compelled to keep competing, even when they’d prefer everyone to slow down or change direction? I’m much less certain about that than about whether the technology will improve.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether greater coordination ability will let people choose a future or merely pursue existing incentives. It does not identify whether human influence will persist long enough to shape the development of that ability.
